title: Now What?
summary: Chapter 21 closes Practical Vim by urging readers to keep practicing until Vim commands become second nature and to pick the book up again, since it is not designed for a single linear pass. It then encourages making Vim your own through a personal vimrc, while insisting that you first learn stock Vim’s baseline behavior—learn to use the saw before sharpening it—and closes with Vim’s charityware license. Note that the assigned range 11753-11976 runs past the chapter body’s end at 11798 into Appendix 1, "Customize Vim to Suit Your Preferences," so the command and concept entries include appendix material.

concepts.name: Shorthand option names
concepts.evidence: Most of Vim’s options also have a shorthand version. The ‘ignorecase’ setting can be abbreviated to ic, so we could toggle this feature by running :se ic! or disable it with :se noic. I tend to use shorthand option names for convenience when customizing Vim on the fly, but I prefer to use the longhand names in my vimrc for the sake of readability.

concepts.name: :setlocal scoping (buffer/window-local options)
concepts.evidence: The :setlocal command scopes the change to the current window or buffer (unless the option can only be set globally). If we were to run :set number, it would enable line numbering for the current window as well as set a new global default. Existing windows would retain their local settings, but new windows would adopt the new global setting.

concepts.name: :source executes each line as an Ex command
concepts.evidence: We can save our customizations by writing them to a file. Then we can use the :source {file} command to apply the settings from the specified {file} to our current editing session (:sourceⓘ). When sourcing a file, Vim executes each line as an Ex command, just as though it had been entered in Command-Line mode.

concepts.name: Autocommands and the FileType event
concepts.evidence: The autocmd declaration tells Vim to listen for an event and to execute the specified commands whenever that event fires (:autocmdⓘ). In this case we’re listening for the FileType event, which is triggered when Vim detects the type of the current file.

concepts.name: ftplugin mechanism
concepts.evidence: This file is just like a regular vimrc, except that the settings will only be applied to JavaScript files. We could also create a ftplugin/ruby.vim file for Ruby customizations and another for each file type that we work with regularly. For more details, look up ftplugin-nameⓘ.
